title: Dynamic Programming and Greedy Algorithms: Choosing Well, Reusing Work

questions.question: Which two properties must a problem have to fit dynamic programming?
questions.rationale: DP fits when the same smaller cases recur (overlapping subproblems) and optimal answers build on optimal sub-answers (optimal substructure).

questions.question: What distinguishes memoization from tabulation?
options: Memoization is bottom-up; tabulation is top-down
Memoization is top-down recursion with a cache; tabulation fills a table with loops
Memoization computes every state; tabulation caches nothing
questions.rationale: Memoization is recursion plus a cache that only computes the states actually needed; tabulation is bottom-up loop-driven and computes every state up to n.

questions.question: In the knapsack walkthrough (capacity 5; A w2 v3, B w3 v4, C w4 v5, D w5 v6), what is the best achievable value?
questions.rationale: The bottom-right table cell holds 7, achieved by taking items A and B — total weight 2 + 3 = 5, total value 3 + 4 = 7.

questions.question: What does the 0/1 knapsack DP table cost to fill, for n items and capacity W?
questions.rationale: The table has one row per item and one column per capacity value, so filling it costs O(n·W).

questions.question: What is the length of the longest common subsequence of "ACE" and "ABCDE"?
questions.rationale: The DP table's bottom-right cell is 3: the subsequence is exactly "ACE", and LCS costs O(m·n) to compute.

questions.question: With coins {1, 3, 4} and amount 6, what does greedy produce and what is optimal?
options: Greedy fails to find any answer
questions.rationale: Greedy grabs the largest coin 4 and limps to 4+1+1 = 3 coins, while the optimum is 3+3 = 2 coins — proof that greedy needs a correctness proof.

questions.question: The greedy-choice property says that:
options: Every local choice is always safe
A locally optimal choice can always be extended to a globally optimal solution
questions.rationale: When a locally optimal choice extends to a globally optimal solution, a greedy algorithm — take the best local option, never revisit — is correct.

questions.question: Which greedy rule solves activity selection?
options: Pick the activity that starts earliest
Pick the activity that finishes earliest
questions.rationale: Picking the activity that finishes earliest is safe because it blocks the fewest others.

questions.question: Which of these is a classic greedy algorithm rather than a DP problem?
questions.rationale: The fractional knapsack is greedily solvable — take items by best value per unit weight — because fractions fill the remainder exactly.

questions.question: A problem phrased as 'count the ways' or 'minimum cost to reach' signals which technique?
questions.rationale: The decision table maps counting-ways, minimum-cost-to-reach, and longest-X phrasings to dynamic programming.
